# Introduction

Environmental heterogeneity can help explain where tree species occur, how
communities change across a plot, and whether different size groups occupy
similar environments. A habitat classification summarizes this heterogeneity
into a small number of classes. Here a habitat is an **operational class of
spatial units**, defined from environmental measurements, sometimes with
composition helping determine the partition. A class need not be a discrete
natural community, a contiguous patch, or a species' physiological niche.

Two forest applications illustrate the distinction. Harms et al. (2001) tested
tree associations with independently defined topographic habitats at Barro
Colorado Island (BCI). John et al. (2007) related tree distributions to soil
resources in three Neotropical plots, using another spatial null model. These
studies motivate examining environmental heterogeneity; they do not establish
one universally correct classification or one interchangeable association test.
Continuous species–environment models remain appropriate when the question
does not require categories.

This tutorial separates **fitting a map** from **testing associations with a
fixed map**. It uses existing R implementations rather than introducing a new
clustering algorithm. The example starts with one census, one community and
20-m quadrats, then adds optional fuzzy membership, floristic guidance and two
diameter groups. The last worked analysis uses the existing point-torus
translator to classify species as enriched, depleted or inconclusive relative
to random alignments with an environmental habitat map.

## Choose a route

Run the shared preparation once, then choose the recipe you need. The
classification recipes do not require one another, except that the legacy
comparison prepares its own historical metrics. Every main recipe returns
ordinary assignments or membership matrices alongside the package's native fit.
Options appear at the start of the code chunks; comments travel with copied code.

| Your purpose | Read and run | Main result |
|---|---|---|
| Start from this plot's raw files | [Data and shared objects](#sec-preparation) | Aligned environment, composition, quadrats and individuals |
| Recover CTFS/fgeo behaviour | [Legacy classification](#sec-legacy) | `habitat.raw` |
| Fit hard environmental classes | [Standardized hierarchy](#sec-hclust) | `habitat.hclust` |
| Retain transitional memberships | [FANNY](#sec-fanny) | `membership.fanny`, `habitat.fanny` |
| Let composition inform environmental rules | [Floristic tree](#sec-ctree) | `habitat.ctree`, `floristic.tree` |
| Understand a probabilistic alternative | [Regions of Common Profile](#sec-rcp) | Optional package workflow |
| Fit separate maps for two diameter groups | [Two size classes](#sec-size) | `habitats.by.size` |
| Store or extract a categorical layer | [Habitat layers](#sec-storage) | `habitat.raster`, categorical fractions |
| Diagnose a small set of maps | [Bounded comparison](#sec-comparison) | One compact diagnostic table |
| Test species against an existing fixed map | [Torus association](#sec-association) | `association`, `null.statistics` |

## Decisions that change the ecological question

| Axis | Choices to state |
|---|---|
| Definition | Environmental resemblance; composition-guided environmental rules; expert-defined classes |
| Population | All eligible individuals; species subsets; species × diameter groups; one census or a stated temporal summary |
| Response | Abundance, presence–absence, basal area or another explicit weight |
| Spatial support | Quadrat grain, sampled extent, complete versus missing effort |
| Environmental geometry | Variables, units, transformations, scaling, correlated gradients, mixed categorical measurements |
| Assignment | One hard label; fuzzy affiliation; model-based membership probability |
| Resolution | Number of assemblages M; classes within each map; minimum class support; transition zones or unclassified sites |
| Space and transfer | Disconnected environmental classes or contiguous zones; local description or prediction to other times/plots |

M denotes the number of separately analysed assemblages, not the number of
habitats. With M = 1 there is one map; with M = 2 there are two, each potentially
with a different number of classes. Fuzzy memberships, latent-class
probabilities and uncertainty in a fitted map are different quantities. None
should be interpreted as another merely because its rows sum to one.

# Data and shared objects {#sec-preparation}

## Set up the example

The supplied BCI files contain the first census (nominally 1982, measured during
1981–1983) and elevation observations. The census team includes Stephen P.
Hubbell, Robin B. Foster, Richard Condit and collaborators at Smithsonian/
ForestGEO. These are historical exports already distributed with fgeo2; their
exact archive release is undocumented. The later Condit et al. (2019) Dryad
archive documents the BCI data conventions, including diameters in millimetres.
See [dataset notes](../../data_examples/README.md) for provenance and licensing.

Run from the repository root or this tutorial's folder. Set `path.to.fgeo2`
explicitly when copying code elsewhere. Outputs go to a temporary folder by
default; set `output.dir` to a persistent folder to reuse them after closing R.
Preparing the terrain requires `interp`
and `FNN` through `derive_topography()`; the remaining native recipes use
`cluster`, `partykit`, `terra`, and `indicspecies`. `withr` and `jsonlite` support
the optional archived-code comparison.

```{r}
#| label: habitat-setup
#| results: hide
#| message: false

path.to.fgeo2 = if(file.exists("../../fgeo2.Rproj")) "../.." else "."
# path.to.fgeo2 = "/full/path/to/fgeo2"
input.dir = file.path(path.to.fgeo2, "data_examples")
output.dir = file.path(tempdir(), "fgeo2-habitats")
plot.extent = c(0, 1000, 0, 500)  # xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax; metres.
quadrat.size = 20
minimum.dbh.cm = 1
census.file = "census1.txt"

# Install once if needed:
# install.packages(c("terra", "interp", "FNN", "cluster", "partykit",
#                    "indicspecies", "withr", "jsonlite"))
library(terra)
library(cluster)
library(partykit)
library(indicspecies)
dir.create(output.dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
models <- list()  # Native fits; each optional recipe adds its own entry.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5,
	message = FALSE, collapse = TRUE)

source(file.path(path.to.fgeo2, "03_spatial/R/new/quadrats.R"))
source(file.path(path.to.fgeo2, "03_spatial/R/new/spatial-null-models.R"))
source(file.path(path.to.fgeo2,
	"06_topography_habitat/R/new/topography-variables.R"))
```

## Define the counted population

Count one eligible living individual per `TreeID`, represented by its largest
living measured stem. This explicit convention avoids counting multi-stemmed
trees several times. It does not reproduce every historical main-stem choice
and must not be carried into growth calculations without matching stem identity.
An all-stems analysis is also legitimate, but has a different target. Report
status, diameter and coordinate exclusions with the results.

```{r}
#| label: habitat-individuals

living.status = "alive"
dbh.to.cm = 0.1                 # This BCI export stores DBH in mm.

# Read identifiers as text, preserving leading zeros.
census <- read.delim(file.path(input.dir, census.file),
	colClasses = c(TreeID = "character", StemID = "character",
		Tag = "character", StemTag = "character", Quadrat = "character"))
keep <- census$Status %in% living.status & is.finite(census$DBH) &
	census$DBH * dbh.to.cm >= minimum.dbh.cm & is.finite(census$PX) &
	is.finite(census$PY) & !is.na(census$Mnemonic) & nzchar(census$Mnemonic)
eligible <- census[keep, ]
eligible <- eligible[order(eligible$TreeID, -eligible$DBH, eligible$StemID), ]
eligible <- eligible[!duplicated(eligible$TreeID), ]
individuals <- data.frame(individual_id = eligible$TreeID,
	x = eligible$PX, y = eligible$PY, species = eligible$Mnemonic,
	dbh_cm = eligible$DBH * dbh.to.cm)
stopifnot(!anyNA(individuals$individual_id),
	!anyDuplicated(individuals$individual_id),
	all(individuals$x >= plot.extent[1] & individuals$x <= plot.extent[2]),
	all(individuals$y >= plot.extent[3] & individuals$y <= plot.extent[4]))
data.frame(stem.rows = nrow(census), eligible.stem.rows = sum(keep),
	counted.individuals = nrow(individuals),
	species = length(unique(individuals$species)))
```

## Make the quadrat-by-species matrix

Spatial grain and diameter cutoffs affect compositional summaries
(Martínez-Villa et al., 2020). The 20-m grain is an exposed starting point, not
an optimized resolution. Retain empty sampled quadrats as zero rows. Missing
sampling effort is not a zero. Point coordinates use the plot's actual bounds,
not minima and maxima inferred from occupied locations.

```{r}
#| label: habitat-composition

boundary.rule = "left_bottom"

# The full rectangle includes cells with no eligible individuals.
quadrats <- make_quadrats_fast(outer.xmin = plot.extent[1],
	outer.ymin = plot.extent[3], outer.xmax = plot.extent[2],
	outer.ymax = plot.extent[4], quadrat.side.x = quadrat.size,
	quadrat.side.y = quadrat.size)
rownames(quadrats) <- quadrats$quadrat_id
membership <- assign_points_to_quadrats(outer.x = individuals$x,
	outer.y = individuals$y, point.id = individuals$individual_id,
	quadrat.locations = quadrats, boundary.rule = boundary.rule)
individuals$quadrat_id <- membership$quadrat_id[
	match(individuals$individual_id, membership$point_id)]
stopifnot(!anyNA(individuals$quadrat_id), nrow(membership) == nrow(individuals))

species.codes <- sort(unique(individuals$species))
composition <- table(
	factor(individuals$quadrat_id, levels = quadrats$quadrat_id),
	factor(individuals$species, levels = species.codes))
dimnames(composition) <- list(quadrat_id = quadrats$quadrat_id,
	species = species.codes)
composition <- unclass(composition)  # Keep a plain numeric matrix, not a table.
stopifnot(sum(composition) == nrow(individuals))
c(quadrats = nrow(composition), species = ncol(composition),
	individuals = sum(composition), empty.quadrats = sum(rowSums(composition) == 0))
```

## Match the environmental table

This brief preparation reuses the completed
[topography](derive-topographical-variables.qmd) and
[environmental extraction](environmental-extraction.qmd) workflows. It makes
5-m terrain layers and averages them within the matching 20-m grid. Elevation,
slope and TPI are the default classification features. TPI is a
neighbourhood-relative elevation measure, not the CTFS convexity formula.
Northness and eastness remain available without treating circular aspect as a
linear variable. Do not add them automatically as extra votes for topography.

```{r}
#| label: habitat-environment

terrain.resolution = 5
position.radius = 20            # TPI square-neighbourhood radius, metres.
fill.missing = TRUE              # Retain the fill mask for provenance.

# This short aggregation route assumes aligned square grids of divisible size.
stopifnot(quadrat.size %% terrain.resolution == 0,
	diff(plot.extent[1:2]) %% quadrat.size == 0,
	diff(plot.extent[3:4]) %% quadrat.size == 0)
xyz <- read.csv(file.path(input.dir, "bci-elevation.csv"))
terrain <- derive_topography(xyz = xyz,
	variables = c("slope", "tpi", "northness", "eastness"),
	resolution = terrain.resolution, extent = plot.extent, crs = "local",
	position.radius = position.radius, fill.missing = fill.missing)
terrain.filled <- attr(terrain, "filled.cells")
terrain.quadrats <- aggregate(terrain,
	fact = quadrat.size / terrain.resolution, fun = "mean", na.rm = TRUE)
quadrat.xy <- cbind(x = (quadrats$xmin + quadrats$xmax) / 2,
	y = (quadrats$ymin + quadrats$ymax) / 2)
environment <- as.data.frame(terra::extract(terrain.quadrats, quadrat.xy))
rownames(environment) <- quadrats$quadrat_id
stopifnot(identical(rownames(environment), rownames(composition)),
	all(is.finite(as.matrix(environment))))
summary(environment[, c("elevation_m", "slope_deg", "tpi_m")])
```

For other data, join each environmental variable by stable quadrat ID before
reordering to `quadrats$quadrat_id`. Soil, canopy and disturbance variables can
be added to this same table. Check dates, units, sampling support and missing
coverage. The supplied BCI soil measurements date from 2010 (Wolf et al., 2015):
using them with 1982 composition assumes a persistent environmental template.
They are not contemporaneous measurements. A complete rectangular terrain map
keeps the core torus example free of soil-interpolation boundary gaps.

## Start here with your own prepared objects

| Object | Rows / columns | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `environment` | N × P | Selected environmental measurements; numeric for the core recipes |
| `composition` | N × S | Raw counts of eligible individuals; retain this before transformations |
| `quadrats` | N rows | Stable `quadrat_id` and rectangle bounds |
| `individuals` | One row per counted individual | Coordinates, species and optional diameter / census features |

All N-row objects refer to the same spatial units **in the same order**. Fitting
needs `environment` and, for floristic methods, `composition`. The continuous
point-torus test additionally needs the original `individuals`: quadrat counts
alone cannot reconstruct point locations. For arbitrary site geometry, the
classification recipes still work, but the rectangular torus recipe does not.
With prepared inputs, run the setup chunk for packages, paths and `models`, then
skip the BCI preparation and enter your chosen method. The independent torus
entry below has its own load-and-source recipe and does not need those packages.

```{r}
#| label: save-habitat-inputs

inputs.file = file.path(output.dir, "habitat-inputs.rds")

saveRDS(list(environment = environment, composition = composition,
	quadrats = quadrats, individuals = individuals, plot.extent = plot.extent),
	inputs.file)
# In another script: inputs <- readRDS(inputs.file)
# environment <- inputs$environment; composition <- inputs$composition
# quadrats <- inputs$quadrats; individuals <- inputs$individuals
# plot.extent <- inputs$plot.extent
```

### More than one census

For a later census, rerun the population and composition preparation using the
same grid and counting rules, then align species columns explicitly. A fixed
map can describe temporal change. Alternatively, refitting a floristic tree
addresses whether its environmental partition changes. Shared individuals and
locations mean these censuses are not independent validation samples. Current
diameter classes, baseline cohorts and recruits answer different questions.

Pooling raw records weights long-lived individuals by their number of observed
censuses. A mean quadrat-by-species abundance across complete censuses instead
describes average standing composition. These are different estimands; specify
one before pooling, and retain census-specific matrices. Basal area and
presence–absence are useful alternative **classification responses**; the torus
counting code below specifically expects individual counts.


# Environmental classifications

These methods group quadrats by environmental resemblance. They do not use the
species matrix. Their classes can occupy several disconnected parts of the
plot; none of the methods below requires spatially contiguous classes. Habitat
numbers are labels, not an ordering from favourable to unfavourable conditions.

## Recover the legacy classification explicitly {#sec-legacy}

`fgeo.analyze::fgeo_habitat()` first derives quadrat topography, then applies
Euclidean distance to **unscaled** mean elevation, convexity and slope,
complete-linkage hierarchical clustering, and a cut into a supplied number of
classes. This is the repository's legacy clustering workflow; it should not be
confused with the expert-defined BCI habitat map used by Harms et al. (2001).

First recover the original quadrat topography, then source the archived
clustering stage with the repository's snapshot loader. The historical functions
expect a zero-origin regular grid, as in this BCI example. This works without installing the full
`fgeo.analyze` suite; the unchanged stage requires `withr`. The direct `stats`
calculation retains the tree, which the legacy output omits.

```{r}
#| label: legacy-topography-inputs
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Recover and align archived CTFS topography"

legacy.commit = "0a2c01dd560daacba0fdc2eb8c9280e2b9d2ea9d"

source(file.path(path.to.fgeo2, "evaluation/0-code-to-source.r"))
legacy <- new.env()
load_github_snapshot(commit = legacy.commit,
	scripts = c("evaluation/Condit/spatial/quadfunc.r",
		"evaluation/Condit/topography/slope.r"), envir = legacy)
legacy.xyz <- xyz[order(xyz$x, xyz$y), ]
names(legacy.xyz)[names(legacy.xyz) == "z"] <- "elev"
legacy.topography <- legacy$allquadratslopes(list(col = legacy.xyz),
	gridsize = quadrat.size, plotdim = c(diff(plot.extent[1:2]),
		diff(plot.extent[3:4])), edgecorrect = TRUE)

# Verify the legacy x-then-y ordering against the four corners of each cell.
xyz.keys <- paste(xyz$x, xyz$y)
corner.elevations <- cbind(
	xyz$z[match(paste(quadrats$xmin, quadrats$ymin), xyz.keys)],
	xyz$z[match(paste(quadrats$xmin, quadrats$ymax), xyz.keys)],
	xyz$z[match(paste(quadrats$xmax, quadrats$ymin), xyz.keys)],
	xyz$z[match(paste(quadrats$xmax, quadrats$ymax), xyz.keys)])
stopifnot(nrow(legacy.topography) == nrow(quadrats),
	max(abs(legacy.topography$meanelev - rowMeans(corner.elevations))) < 1e-7)
rownames(legacy.topography) <- quadrats$quadrat_id
```

```{r}
#| label: legacy-habitat-clustering
#| message: false

habitat.k = 4L
legacy.commit = "d69bfe711263305fcbaf322d402eba2f1edfb084"

source(file.path(path.to.fgeo2, "evaluation/0-code-to-source.r"))
legacy.clustering <- new.env()
load_github_snapshot(repo = "forestgeo/fgeo.analyze", commit = legacy.commit,
	scripts = "R/add_cluster.R", envir = legacy.clustering)

# The preparation section checks these rows against the original quadrat index.
legacy.metrics <- legacy.topography[, c("meanelev", "convex", "slope")]
rownames(legacy.metrics) <- quadrats$quadrat_id
if(any(!is.finite(as.matrix(legacy.metrics))))
	stop("Resolve missing legacy topography before this comparison.")

legacy.input <- structure(legacy.metrics,
	class = c("fgeo_topography", "data.frame"))
legacy.result <- legacy.clustering$add_cluster(legacy.input, n = habitat.k)

raw.tree <- hclust(dist(legacy.metrics), method = "complete")
habitat.raw <- cutree(raw.tree, k = habitat.k)
stopifnot(identical(unname(habitat.raw), legacy.result$cluster))
models$raw <- raw.tree
table(habitat.raw)
```

The agreement above isolates the clustering implementation because both calls
receive identical metric values and the same k. Replacing CTFS convexity with
raster TPI also changes the environmental definition; a changed map would then
reflect more than the clustering algorithm. Changing metres to centimetres in
only one raw variable can change the result because raw Euclidean distances
retain the supplied units.

For an installation of `fgeo.analyze`, its original whole workflow remains:

```{r}
#| label: installed-fgeo-habitat
#| eval: false

habitat.k = 4L
quadrat.side = 20
plot.dimensions = c(1000, 500)

# xyz is the original surveyed elevation table, with columns x, y and z.
legacy.xyz <- xyz[order(xyz$x, xyz$y), ]
names(legacy.xyz)[names(legacy.xyz) == "z"] <- "elev"
legacy.habitat <- fgeo.analyze::fgeo_habitat(
	list(col = legacy.xyz, xdim = plot.dimensions[1], ydim = plot.dimensions[2]),
	gridsize = quadrat.side, n = habitat.k, edgecorrect = TRUE)
```

## Standardized environmental hierarchical clustering {#sec-hclust}

Standardizing each selected variable to unit standard deviation changes its
weight in Euclidean distance. This is a sensitivity choice, not an automatic
improvement: it gives equal variance weight to the supplied variables, while
several correlated variables can still emphasize the same gradient. Select
columns for the ecological question before searching for k.

The small candidate set below is screened by mean silhouette width, which
compares within-class resemblance with the nearest alternative class. A larger
value supports separation under this particular distance. It does not prove
that a continuous environmental gradient contains discrete ecological habitats.
Inspect the class sizes and map alongside the diagnostic.

```{r}
#| label: standardized-hierarchical-habitats

environment.columns = c("elevation_m", "slope_deg", "tpi_m")
candidate.k = 2:6
habitat.k = NULL                 # Or set one value after inspecting diagnostics.
minimum.class.quadrats = 10L     # Exposed minimum spatial representation.
linkage = "complete"            # Same linkage as the legacy comparison.
use.pca = FALSE
variance.target = 0.9           # Used only when use.pca = TRUE.

environment.scaled <- scale(environment[, environment.columns, drop = FALSE])
if(any(!is.finite(environment.scaled)))
	stop("Selected variables need complete values and nonzero variance.")

# PCA is optional. Retaining all axes leaves Euclidean distances unchanged.
environment.scores <- environment.scaled
if(use.pca)
{
	environment.pca <- prcomp(environment.scaled, center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE)
	explained <- cumsum(environment.pca$sdev^2) / sum(environment.pca$sdev^2)
	number.axes <- which(explained >= variance.target)[1]
	environment.scores <- environment.pca$x[, seq_len(number.axes), drop = FALSE]
}

environment.distance <- dist(environment.scores)
cluster.tree <- hclust(environment.distance, method = linkage)
if(any(candidate.k < 2 | candidate.k >= nrow(environment)))
	stop("Candidate k values must be between 2 and N - 1.")

cluster.diagnostics <- data.frame(k = candidate.k, mean.silhouette = NA_real_,
	smallest.class = NA_integer_)
for(j in seq_along(candidate.k))
{
	groups <- cutree(cluster.tree, k = candidate.k[j])
	widths <- silhouette(groups, environment.distance)
	cluster.diagnostics$mean.silhouette[j] <- mean(widths[, "sil_width"])
	cluster.diagnostics$smallest.class[j] <- min(table(groups))
}
eligible <- cluster.diagnostics$smallest.class >= minimum.class.quadrats
cluster.diagnostics$eligible <- eligible
print(cluster.diagnostics)
if(!any(eligible)) stop("No candidate partition satisfies minimum.class.quadrats.")
if(is.null(habitat.k))
{
	scores <- cluster.diagnostics$mean.silhouette
	scores[!eligible] <- -Inf
	habitat.k <- candidate.k[which.max(scores)]
}
selected <- match(habitat.k, candidate.k)
if(is.na(selected) || !eligible[selected])
	stop("Choose an eligible k from the hierarchical diagnostic table.")

habitat.hclust <- cutree(cluster.tree, k = habitat.k)
names(habitat.hclust) <- rownames(environment)
models$hclust <- cluster.tree
table(habitat.hclust)
plot(cluster.diagnostics$k, cluster.diagnostics$mean.silhouette,
	type = "b", xlab = "Number of classes", ylab = "Mean silhouette width")
```

To isolate the effect of scaling, repeat both raw and standardized calls with
the **same three metric columns and k**. To add soils or canopy measurements,
change `environment.columns`; inspect skewed variables and use a stated
transformation when needed. The minimum class size states the smallest
acceptable spatial representation; it is not a biological constant. The
default still allows small groups, so inspect the reported sizes and map.
With many correlated numeric predictors, retaining
only some PCA axes is an additional modelling choice. For genuinely mixed
numeric and categorical measurements, a separate option is
`cluster::daisy(..., metric = "gower")` followed by average or complete linkage;
do not turn categories into arbitrary numeric scores or apply Ward's Euclidean
criterion indiscriminately to mixed-data distances.

## Fuzzy environmental classes with FANNY {#sec-fanny}

FANNY, described by Kaufman and Rousseeuw (1990), lets each quadrat have degrees
of affiliation with several classes. Their row sum is one, but these values
are **fuzzy memberships, not occurrence probabilities**. The native object also
contains a nearest hard classification. Preserve both outputs: a hard map hides
quadrats with intermediate memberships.

This comparison uses the same standardized columns independently of the
previous fit. Its bounded k screen describes the nearest hard partitions;
the normalized partition coefficient additionally describes membership
crispness. Neither diagnostic is a universal ecological criterion for k.

```{r}
#| label: fuzzy-environmental-habitats

environment.columns = c("elevation_m", "slope_deg", "tpi_m")
candidate.k = 2:4               # Keep this small: FANNY uses pairwise distances.
habitat.k = NULL
membership.exponent = 1.5       # Larger values make affiliations more diffuse.
maximum.iterations = 500L
convergence.tolerance = 1e-8

environment.scaled <- scale(environment[, environment.columns, drop = FALSE])
if(any(!is.finite(environment.scaled)))
	stop("Selected variables need complete values and nonzero variance.")
if(any(candidate.k < 2 | candidate.k >= nrow(environment) / 2))
	stop("FANNY candidate k values must satisfy 2 <= k < N / 2.")
environment.distance <- dist(environment.scaled)

fuzzy.fits <- vector("list", length(candidate.k))
fuzzy.diagnostics <- data.frame(k = candidate.k, mean.silhouette = NA_real_,
	partition.coefficient = NA_real_, crisp.classes = NA_integer_, converged = FALSE)
for(j in seq_along(candidate.k))
{
	fuzzy.fits[[j]] <- fanny(environment.distance, k = candidate.k[j],
		diss = TRUE, memb.exp = membership.exponent, keep.diss = FALSE,
		maxit = maximum.iterations, tol = convergence.tolerance)
	if(!is.null(fuzzy.fits[[j]]$silinfo$avg.width))
		fuzzy.diagnostics$mean.silhouette[j] <- fuzzy.fits[[j]]$silinfo$avg.width
	fuzzy.diagnostics$partition.coefficient[j] <- fuzzy.fits[[j]]$coeff[2]
	fuzzy.diagnostics$crisp.classes[j] <- fuzzy.fits[[j]]$k.crisp
	fuzzy.diagnostics$converged[j] <- fuzzy.fits[[j]]$convergence["converged"] == 1
}
print(fuzzy.diagnostics)

# Do not select an unconverged fit or one whose hard classes have collapsed.
eligible <- fuzzy.diagnostics$converged &
	fuzzy.diagnostics$crisp.classes == candidate.k &
	is.finite(fuzzy.diagnostics$mean.silhouette)
if(!any(eligible))
	stop("No eligible FANNY fit; inspect diagnostics and membership.exponent.")
if(is.null(habitat.k))
{
	scores <- fuzzy.diagnostics$mean.silhouette
	scores[!eligible] <- -Inf
	habitat.k <- candidate.k[which.max(scores)]
}
selected <- match(habitat.k, candidate.k)
if(is.na(selected) || !eligible[selected])
	stop("Choose an eligible k from the FANNY diagnostic table.")

fuzzy.fit <- fuzzy.fits[[selected]]
habitat.fanny <- fuzzy.fit$clustering
names(habitat.fanny) <- rownames(environment)
membership.fanny <- fuzzy.fit$membership
rownames(membership.fanny) <- rownames(environment)
colnames(membership.fanny) <- paste0("habitat_", seq_len(ncol(membership.fanny)))
models$fanny <- fuzzy.fit
stopifnot(all(abs(rowSums(membership.fanny) - 1) < 1e-8))
table(habitat.fanny)
summary(apply(membership.fanny, 1, max))
```

If memberships approach 1/k everywhere or fewer hard classes remain than
requested, inspect the warning and try a smaller membership exponent. Values
near one produce crisper solutions and can converge more slowly. Show maximum
membership, or individual membership columns, as well as the hard map.

# Floristically informed classifications

Here community composition helps define the environmental partition. The
resulting map answers a different question from clustering the environment
alone. Keep the sampled population and size threshold explicit: refitting on
another species group or size class can produce another map. Repeating an
environment-only fit on an unchanged environmental matrix cannot change that
map merely because different trees were selected.

## Multivariate conditional inference tree {#sec-ctree}

De'ath (2002) introduced multivariate regression trees for species-environment
relationships. The maintained `partykit::ctree()` implementation below uses the
**conditional inference algorithm of Hothorn, Hornik and Zeileis (2006)**,
which selects splits by association tests. It is not an implementation of
De'ath's sum-of-squares MRT algorithm. Its terminal nodes nevertheless provide
an explicit environmental partition informed by the species matrix.

The Hellinger transformation takes square roots of within-quadrat relative
abundances (Legendre and Gallagher, 2001). This example therefore describes
relative composition rather than total tree density. The species-occurrence
filter is an exposed computational and ecological choice; the denominator
below is the abundance of the retained species. Empty retained communities
are excluded from fitting, while their environmental values can still receive
a model-based prediction.

```{r}
#| label: floristically-informed-tree
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6

environment.columns = c("elevation_m", "slope_deg", "tpi_m")
minimum.occupied.quadrats = 10L
test.statistic = "quadratic"    # Joint multivariate association test.
split.statistic = "maximum"     # Set separately; affects the split search.
tree.seed = 20261120

set.seed(tree.seed)
split.criterion = 0.99
minimum.node.size = 50L
maximum.depth = 3L             # At most 2^maximum.depth terminal classes.

species.keep <- colSums(composition > 0) >= minimum.occupied.quadrats
community <- composition[, species.keep, drop = FALSE]
if(ncol(community) < 2)
	stop("At least two retained species are needed for this multivariate example.")
training.rows <- rowSums(community) > 0
environment.tree <- environment[, environment.columns, drop = FALSE]
if(any(!is.finite(as.matrix(environment.tree))))
	stop("Resolve missing environmental values before fitting or mapping the tree.")

community.hel <- sqrt(sweep(community[training.rows, , drop = FALSE], 1,
	rowSums(community[training.rows, , drop = FALSE]), "/"))

# Separate response columns are supported by native printing and plotting.
# data.frame() makes syntactically valid, unique names for the formula.
floristic.data <- data.frame(community.hel,
	environment.tree[training.rows, , drop = FALSE], check.names = TRUE)
response.names <- names(floristic.data)[seq_len(ncol(community.hel))]
predictor.names <- names(floristic.data)[ncol(community.hel) + seq_len(ncol(environment.tree))]
floristic.formula <- as.formula(paste(paste(response.names, collapse = " + "),
	"~", paste(predictor.names, collapse = " + ")))
floristic.tree <- ctree(floristic.formula, data = floristic.data,
	control = ctree_control(teststat = test.statistic, splitstat = split.statistic,
		testtype = "Bonferroni",
		mincriterion = split.criterion, minbucket = minimum.node.size,
		minsplit = 2L * minimum.node.size, maxdepth = maximum.depth))

# Node IDs are the native hard habitat labels; they need not be consecutive.
prediction.data <- environment.tree
names(prediction.data) <- predictor.names
habitat.ctree <- predict(floristic.tree, newdata = prediction.data, type = "node")
names(habitat.ctree) <- rownames(environment)
models$ctree <- floristic.tree
print(floristic.tree)
table(habitat.ctree)
plot(floristic.tree, type = "simple")
```

The global test uses a quadratic multivariate statistic. The split search uses
the largest standardized component, a separate native control that keeps the
search practical with hundreds of species. Using a quadratic split statistic
is another choice and may be slower. These criteria can yield different trees;
neither is De'ath's sum-of-squares MRT.

The number of classes emerges from stopping, minimum node size and the depth
limit, rather than a supplied k. Inspect the tree and class sizes; rerun a
small, stated sensitivity to these controls if the map is too fragmented or
too coarse for the question. With spatially autocorrelated quadrats, internal
split-test p-values are model-building controls, not independent evidence of
habitat associations. Predictive claims need held-out spatial blocks. Species
summaries made from the same composition used to fit this map are descriptive.

With many response columns, trying `"maximum"` for both statistic options can
make the native calculation substantially faster. This changes the
multivariate criterion and can change the boundaries; it is a modelling
alternative, not a promise to reproduce the quadratic tree more quickly.

For exact De'ath MRT, a revived `aurelienboye/mvpart` fork is available with a
worked ecological example. It is an optional GitHub dependency rather than a
drop-in relabelling of `ctree`; its cross-validation and one-standard-error
tree-size selection belong to that separate workflow.

## Optional: probabilistic Regions of Common Profile {#sec-rcp}

Foster et al. (2013) model groups of sites using both multispecies observations
and environment. `ecomix::regional_mix()` implements these Regions of Common
Profile (RCP). Unlike `ecomix::species_mix()`, it groups **sites**, so it can
produce a habitat-membership matrix. Its fitted `postProbs` use the observed
flora, whereas `pis` and `predict()` give environmental prior probabilities
learned through the fitted model. These are latent-class probabilities, not
FANNY affiliations or proportions of several habitats in a quadrat.

This native template is deliberately **not evaluated** in the core tutorial.
It requires a compiler and the GitHub `ecomix` package, and likelihood searches
can be costly. Install once with
`remotes::install_github("skiptoniam/ecomix@17418626")` and inspect the package's
RCP example before running it. The interface was checked with version 2.0.1,
commit `17418626e5c9e12337a335bbffe1b294e95f924b`, on a small simulated
40-site, 10-species dataset; the full BCI likelihood search is not run here.
Keep untransformed
counts for the negative-binomial family. The short start count below is for
trying the interface; increase it and check that independent starts agree
before relying on BIC to select k.

```{r}
#| label: optional-rcp-habitats
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Optional native RCP template"

environment.columns = c("elevation_m", "slope_deg", "tpi_m")
minimum.occupied.quadrats = 10L
candidate.k = 2:4
number.starts = 10L
seed = 20261120

library(ecomix)
set.seed(seed)
rcp.environment <- as.data.frame(scale(environment[, environment.columns, drop = FALSE]))
species.keep <- colSums(composition > 0) >= minimum.occupied.quadrats
rcp.data <- make_mixture_data(species_data = composition[, species.keep, drop = FALSE],
	covariate_data = rcp.environment)

# Use the constructor and multivariate formula supported by the package source.
# Some regional_mix help text still describes an older list interface.
response.names <- names(rcp.data)[seq_len(sum(species.keep))]
predictor.names <- names(rcp.data)[sum(species.keep) + 1L + seq_len(ncol(rcp.environment))]
names(rcp.environment) <- predictor.names
rcp.formula <- as.formula(paste("cbind(", paste(response.names, collapse = ", "),
	") ~", paste(predictor.names, collapse = " + ")))

rcp.fits <- vector("list", length(candidate.k))
for(j in seq_along(candidate.k))
{
	starts <- regional_mix.multifit(rcp_formula = rcp.formula, species_formula = ~1,
		data = rcp.data, nRCP = candidate.k[j], family = "negative.binomial",
		nstart = number.starts, mc.cores = 1, titbits = TRUE)
	log.likelihood <- sapply(starts$multiple_fits, function(x)
		if(x$conv == 0) x$logl else -Inf)
	if(!any(is.finite(log.likelihood))) stop("No converged RCP start at k = ", candidate.k[j])
	rcp.fits[[j]] <- starts$multiple_fits[[which.max(log.likelihood)]]
}
rcp.diagnostics <- data.frame(k = candidate.k, BIC = sapply(rcp.fits, BIC))
print(rcp.diagnostics)
regional.fit <- rcp.fits[[which.min(rcp.diagnostics$BIC)]]

posterior.rcp <- regional.fit$postProbs
prediction.rcp <- predict(regional.fit, newdata = rcp.environment)
rownames(posterior.rcp) <- rownames(prediction.rcp) <- rownames(environment)
habitat.rcp <- setNames(max.col(posterior.rcp, ties.method = "first"), rownames(environment))
habitat.rcp.environment <- setNames(max.col(prediction.rcp, ties.method = "first"),
	rownames(environment))
models$rcp <- regional.fit
```

Map `posterior.rcp` when describing the observed communities. Map
`prediction.rcp` when describing what the fitted environmental model predicts
at these or new sites. Compare BIC only between converged models fitted to the
same responses and covariate specification, then inspect class sizes, residuals
and stability. RCP, like the other methods here, does not itself impose spatial
contiguity.

## Two maps for two size classes {#sec-size}

To make M = 2, keep the same environmental table and quadrat grid, but rebuild
composition and refit the floristic tree for each stated population. These are
size classes, not universal juvenile/adult categories. Each column of
`habitats.by.size` is a different hard map; its rows retain the same quadrat
IDs. Environmental clustering need not be repeated because its inputs have
not changed. Comita et al. (2007) found differences between small- and large-tree
habitat associations at BCI, motivating size-specific questions without
justifying one universal diameter boundary.

```{r}
#| label: size-specific-floristic-maps

size.breaks = c(1, 10, Inf)       # DBH in cm; left-closed intervals.
size.labels = c("1 to <10 cm", "10 cm or more")
environment.columns = c("elevation_m", "slope_deg", "tpi_m")
minimum.occupied.quadrats = 10L
test.statistic = "quadratic"
split.statistic = "maximum"
tree.seed = 20261120

set.seed(tree.seed)
split.criterion = 0.99
minimum.node.size = 50L
maximum.depth = 3L

size.class <- cut(individuals$dbh_cm, breaks = size.breaks,
	labels = size.labels, right = FALSE)
environment.tree <- environment[, environment.columns, drop = FALSE]
models.by.size <- composition.by.size <- vector("list", length(size.labels))
names(models.by.size) <- names(composition.by.size) <- size.labels
habitats.by.size <- matrix(NA_integer_, nrow(environment), length(size.labels),
	dimnames = list(rownames(environment), size.labels))
size.diagnostics <- data.frame(size.class = size.labels, individuals = NA_integer_,
	retained.species = NA_integer_, training.quadrats = NA_integer_, habitats = NA_integer_)

for(m in seq_along(size.labels))
{
	keep <- !is.na(size.class) & size.class == size.labels[m]
	community <- table(factor(individuals$quadrat_id[keep], levels = quadrats$quadrat_id),
		factor(individuals$species[keep], levels = colnames(composition)))
	community <- unclass(community)
	composition.by.size[[m]] <- community
	species.keep <- colSums(community > 0) >= minimum.occupied.quadrats
	community <- community[, species.keep, drop = FALSE]
	training.rows <- rowSums(community) > 0
	size.diagnostics$individuals[m] <- sum(keep)
	size.diagnostics$retained.species[m] <- ncol(community)
	size.diagnostics$training.quadrats[m] <- sum(training.rows)
	if(ncol(community) < 2 || sum(training.rows) < 2L * minimum.node.size)
	{
		warning("Insufficient composition for size class: ", size.labels[m])
		next
	}

	community.hel <- sqrt(sweep(community[training.rows, , drop = FALSE], 1,
		rowSums(community[training.rows, , drop = FALSE]), "/"))
	floristic.data <- data.frame(community.hel,
		environment.tree[training.rows, , drop = FALSE], check.names = TRUE)
	response.names <- names(floristic.data)[seq_len(ncol(community.hel))]
	predictor.names <- names(floristic.data)[ncol(community.hel) + seq_len(ncol(environment.tree))]
	floristic.formula <- as.formula(paste(paste(response.names, collapse = " + "),
		"~", paste(predictor.names, collapse = " + ")))
	models.by.size[[m]] <- ctree(floristic.formula, data = floristic.data,
		control = ctree_control(teststat = test.statistic, splitstat = split.statistic,
			testtype = "Bonferroni",
			mincriterion = split.criterion, minbucket = minimum.node.size,
			minsplit = 2L * minimum.node.size, maxdepth = maximum.depth))
	prediction.data <- environment.tree
	names(prediction.data) <- predictor.names
	habitats.by.size[, m] <- predict(models.by.size[[m]],
		newdata = prediction.data, type = "node")
	size.diagnostics$habitats[m] <- length(unique(habitats.by.size[, m]))
}
print(size.diagnostics)
```

Do not compare node numbers across these fits as if they named the same habitat.
Compare the maps, split rules and environmental profiles. Reusing the same flora
to fit and describe either map still gives a descriptive comparison, so these
two fitted maps do not supply an independent size-specific association test.
The separate occurrence filters also retain different species panels and
Hellinger denominators. Differences reflect species turnover, sample size and
filtering as well as size-related environmental pattern. When asking about
within-species size responses, compare a shared species panel as a sensitivity.

# Choose a map for the common downstream workflow

Every evaluated method above leaves a named integer vector in quadrat order.
Choose one explicitly for mapping, community summaries and the later fixed-map
torus demonstration; retain the method-specific objects to compare alternatives.

```{r}
#| label: choose-habitat-classification

selected.map = "standardized hclust"
selected.features = c("elevation_m", "slope_deg", "tpi_m")
map.uses.test.flora = FALSE      # TRUE if the association species helped fit/select it.

habitats <- habitat.hclust
# habitats <- habitat.raw
# habitats <- habitat.fanny
# habitats <- habitat.ctree
# For the floristic tree, also set map.uses.test.flora = TRUE above.

stopifnot(identical(names(habitats), quadrats$quadrat_id),
	length(habitats) == nrow(composition), !anyNA(habitats))
```

The selected map can be reused without rerunning its fit. Save the native model
and its preprocessing choices alongside the assignments; save fuzzy memberships
or RCP probabilities separately when using them. Selecting a flora-informed
map changes the interpretation of any subsequent species-association summary.

```{r}
#| label: habitat-environmental-profiles

profile.columns = c("elevation_m", "slope_deg", "tpi_m")

# Read class numbers through area and environmental measurements, not their order.
profiles <- expand.grid(habitat = sort(unique(as.character(habitats))),
	variable = profile.columns, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
profiles$area.ha <- NA_real_
profiles$median <- NA_real_
profiles$q25 <- NA_real_
profiles$q75 <- NA_real_
for(i in seq_len(nrow(profiles)))
{
	keep <- as.character(habitats) == profiles$habitat[i]
	values <- environment[keep, profiles$variable[i]]
	profiles$area.ha[i] <- sum((quadrats$xmax[keep] - quadrats$xmin[keep]) *
		(quadrats$ymax[keep] - quadrats$ymin[keep])) / 10000
	profiles$median[i] <- median(values)
	profiles$q25[i] <- quantile(values, 0.25)
	profiles$q75[i] <- quantile(values, 0.75)
}
knitr::kable(profiles, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
```

Use these profiles for provisional descriptions such as lower-elevation steep
terrain or relatively elevated, gentle terrain. Preserve the measured ranges:
an attractive name can hide substantial overlap between classes. These labels
describe the environmental partition, not which species should prefer it.
With the supplied standardized BCI defaults, classes 4 and 5 occupy 18.2 and
19.6 ha, with median elevations of about 141.2 and 152.0 m and gentle median
slopes. Classes 1 and 3 cover only 0.60 and 0.52 ha: both are steep, but their
median TPI has opposite signs. That small spatial support deserves attention
when interpreting their species associations.

```{r}
#| label: save-fixed-habitat-map

fixed.map.file = file.path(output.dir, "fixed-map-inputs.rds")

# This checkpoint is sufficient for the independent torus route below.
saveRDS(list(quadrats = quadrats, composition = composition, habitats = habitats,
	individuals = individuals, plot.extent = plot.extent,
	map.uses.test.flora = map.uses.test.flora), fixed.map.file)
```


# Habitat layers and spatial coherence {#sec-storage}

Similarity in environment does not imply geographical adjacency. Several
disconnected slopes may reasonably share one class. Contiguous zones answer
a different mapping objective: packages such as `adespatial` offer spatially
constrained methods, whereas posthoc smoothing changes an existing partition.
This section stores the original map and offers one explicit sensitivity filter.
Neither a neighbourhood penalty nor a majority filter necessarily guarantees
that every habitat forms one connected region.

## Store a categorical layer

Run after choosing `habitats`; this section needs only `quadrats`, `habitats`,
and `individuals`, not a fitted model. Classes are nominal: a mean of their
numeric codes has no ecological interpretation. An explicit key preserves
arbitrary labels, including nonconsecutive tree-node numbers or text labels.

```{r}
#| label: categorical-habitat-raster
# output.dir = "/full/path/to/outputs"  # Otherwise retain the setup's folder.
overwrite.outputs = FALSE

# Requires: one named habitat label for every cell of a complete regular grid.
stopifnot(identical(names(habitats), quadrats$quadrat_id), !anyNA(habitats))
cell.width <- unique(quadrats$xmax - quadrats$xmin)
cell.height <- unique(quadrats$ymax - quadrats$ymin)
stopifnot(length(cell.width) == 1, length(cell.height) == 1)
habitat.raster <- terra::rast(xmin = min(quadrats$xmin),
    xmax = max(quadrats$xmax), ymin = min(quadrats$ymin),
    ymax = max(quadrats$ymax), resolution = c(cell.width, cell.height), crs = "")
quadrat.xy <- cbind((quadrats$xmin + quadrats$xmax) / 2,
    (quadrats$ymin + quadrats$ymax) / 2)
quadrat.cells <- terra::cellFromXY(habitat.raster, quadrat.xy)
stopifnot(!anyNA(quadrat.cells), !anyDuplicated(quadrat.cells),
    length(quadrat.cells) == terra::ncell(habitat.raster),
    max(abs(quadrat.xy - terra::xyFromCell(habitat.raster, quadrat.cells))) <
        min(cell.width, cell.height) * 1e-8)

# Use cell indexes: quadrat order need not be raster order (north to south).
habitat.labels <- sort(unique(as.character(habitats)))
habitat.key <- data.frame(habitat_code = seq_along(habitat.labels),
    habitat_label = habitat.labels)
raster.codes <- rep(NA_integer_, terra::ncell(habitat.raster))
raster.codes[quadrat.cells] <- match(as.character(habitats), habitat.labels)
terra::values(habitat.raster) <- raster.codes
levels(habitat.raster) <- habitat.key
names(habitat.raster) <- "habitat_code"
stopifnot(identical(habitat.key$habitat_label[
    terra::values(habitat.raster)[quadrat.cells, 1]], as.character(habitats)))

dir.create(output.dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
terra::writeRaster(habitat.raster, file.path(output.dir, "habitat-map.tif"),
    datatype = "INT4S", overwrite = overwrite.outputs)
write.csv(habitat.key, file.path(output.dir, "habitat-key.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(data.frame(quadrat_id = quadrats$quadrat_id, cell = quadrat.cells,
    habitat_code = raster.codes[quadrat.cells]),
    file.path(output.dir, "habitat-quadrats.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
plot(habitat.raster, main = "Chosen habitat classification")
if(exists("terrain.filled") && !is.null(terrain.filled))
	writeRaster(terrain.filled, file.path(output.dir, "terrain-filled-cells.tif"),
		overwrite = overwrite.outputs)
```

Coordinates remain in the plot's local metres (`crs = ""`). Do not attach a
geographic CRS without a real coordinate transformation. Keep the GeoTIFF and
its sidecar files together; the CSV key also documents the code-to-label mapping.

## Optional: one modal-filter sensitivity map

This replaces every cell simultaneously with its 3 × 3 neighbourhood mode,
including the focal cell. Outside-grid neighbours are missing and ignored;
there is no toroidal wrapping. Ties choose the lowest storage code, an arbitrary
but reproducible convention. This can erase small real habitats, so retain the
original and compare results rather than assuming smoothing improves the map.

```{r}
#| label: optional-modal-habitat-map
run.modal.filter = FALSE
tie.rule = "lowest"

# Requires the stored raster/key, quadrat.cells and the original habitats.
if(run.modal.filter)
{
    # The nine layers all come from the original map: one synchronous pass.
    neighbourhood <- terra::rast(habitat.raster, nlyrs = 9)
    terra::values(neighbourhood) <- terra::focalValues(habitat.raster, w = 3, fill = NA)
    habitat.raster.modal <- terra::modal(neighbourhood, ties = tie.rule, na.rm = TRUE)
    levels(habitat.raster.modal) <- habitat.key
    names(habitat.raster.modal) <- "habitat_code"
    filtered.codes <- terra::values(habitat.raster.modal)[quadrat.cells, 1]
    habitat.modal <- habitat.key$habitat_label[filtered.codes]
    names(habitat.modal) <- names(habitats)
    print(c(changed_cells = sum(habitat.modal != as.character(habitats)),
        changed_fraction = mean(habitat.modal != as.character(habitats))))
    print(table(original = as.character(habitats), filtered = habitat.modal))
    plot(habitat.raster.modal, main = "One modal-filter pass")
}
```

`habitats` and `habitat.raster` remain the selected original map. To analyse the
filtered map, explicitly select `habitat.modal` as a separate sensitivity analysis.

## Points

For the prepared census, retained quadrat IDs give exactly the original boundary
convention. For new points use simple categorical extraction, never bilinear
interpolation. `terra` assigns a point on an internal horizontal grid line to
the cell below; the preparation's bottom-inclusive rule assigns it above.
Use the existing quadrat-assignment recipe first when matching that convention.

```{r}
#| label: extract-habitat-at-points
point.rows = seq_len(min(5L, nrow(individuals)))

# Census lookup preserves the assignments used to build composition.
census.habitats <- data.frame(individual_id = individuals$individual_id,
    habitat_label = as.character(habitats)[
        match(individuals$quadrat_id, quadrats$quadrat_id)])

# Replace these example coordinates with new query points in local metres.
query.points <- terra::vect(individuals[point.rows, c("x", "y"), drop = FALSE],
    geom = c("x", "y"), crs = "")
point.codes <- terra::extract(habitat.raster, query.points,
    method = "simple", ID = FALSE, raw = TRUE)[, 1]
point.habitats <- data.frame(point_row = point.rows, habitat_code = point.codes,
    habitat_label = habitat.key$habitat_label[match(point.codes, habitat.key$habitat_code)])
point.habitats
```

## Buffers, quadrats and arbitrary polygons

The same recipe gives class areas for all three geometries. Fractions below use
the **mapped part** of each geometry as denominator; outside-map area is excluded.
An absent class has zero area; a geometry with no mapped overlap has `NA` fractions.
Overlapping query regions are summarised separately. `exact = TRUE` weights each
class by the fraction of each raster cell covered by the query polygon.

```{r}
#| label: extract-habitat-area-fractions
buffer.rows = c(1L, 2L)
buffer.radius.m = 25
quadrat.rows = c(1L, 2L)
polygon.wkt = "POLYGON ((100 100, 200 100, 150 200, 100 100))"

# Requires the stored map/key; geometry coordinates use the same local metres.
buffer.points <- terra::vect(individuals[buffer.rows, c("x", "y"), drop = FALSE],
    geom = c("x", "y"), crs = "")
buffers <- terra::buffer(buffer.points, width = buffer.radius.m)
terra::values(buffers) <- data.frame(region_id = paste0("buffer_", buffer.rows))
quadrat.polygons <- terra::as.polygons(habitat.raster,
    aggregate = FALSE, values = FALSE)[quadrat.cells[quadrat.rows], ]
terra::values(quadrat.polygons) <- data.frame(
    region_id = paste0("quadrat_", quadrats$quadrat_id[quadrat.rows]))
polygons <- terra::vect(polygon.wkt, crs = "")
terra::values(polygons) <- data.frame(region_id = paste0("polygon_", seq_len(nrow(polygons))))
regions <- rbind(buffers, quadrat.polygons, polygons)

overlap <- as.data.frame(terra::extract(habitat.raster, regions,
    exact = TRUE, raw = TRUE))
keep <- !is.na(overlap$habitat_code) & is.finite(overlap$fraction) & overlap$fraction > 0
overlap <- overlap[keep, , drop = FALSE]
overlap$area_m2 <- overlap$fraction * prod(terra::res(habitat.raster))
areas <- data.frame(ID = integer(), habitat_code = integer(), area_m2 = numeric())
if(nrow(overlap) > 0)
    areas <- aggregate(area_m2 ~ ID + habitat_code, data = overlap, FUN = sum)

# Include zero-area classes and preserve query regions with no overlap.
area.fractions <- merge(expand.grid(ID = seq_len(nrow(regions)),
    habitat_code = habitat.key$habitat_code), areas, all.x = TRUE)
area.fractions$area_m2[is.na(area.fractions$area_m2)] <- 0
area.fractions$mapped_area_m2 <- ave(area.fractions$area_m2, area.fractions$ID, FUN = sum)
area.fractions$fraction_mapped <- NA_real_
has.area <- area.fractions$mapped_area_m2 > 0
area.fractions$fraction_mapped[has.area] <- area.fractions$area_m2[has.area] /
    area.fractions$mapped_area_m2[has.area]
area.fractions$region_id <- regions$region_id[area.fractions$ID]
area.fractions$habitat_label <- habitat.key$habitat_label[
    match(area.fractions$habitat_code, habitat.key$habitat_code)]
area.fractions[, c("region_id", "habitat_label", "area_m2",
    "mapped_area_m2", "fraction_mapped")]
```

For FANNY, keep all columns of `membership.fanny` alongside the hard map. On this
same grid, place each column into a raster layer through `quadrat.cells`, as
above, and save the stack as continuous memberships. Weighted polygon means
then describe mean affiliation, not the area of a hard habitat. Model-based
probabilities can use the same storage pattern, with their distinct meaning
recorded. Avoid bilinear interpolation of hard habitat codes.


# A bounded diagnostic comparison {#sec-comparison}

Compare a few plausible maps on the same quadrats, rather than treating every
combination of M, k, predictors and smoothing as a tournament. The table below
asks whether a partition is adequately represented, separates a **common**
environmental space and has recognizable indicator species. These are
diagnostics, not independent validation or a universal ranking of methods.
More classes usually improve within-class fit; that alone does not justify
their complexity.

The indicator calculation uses the group-equalized `IndVal.g` of
`indicspecies`. It combines specificity and fidelity to groups of sites; the
package reports its square root. A species can indicate a combination of
habitats rather than a single one (De Cáceres et al., 2010). Here, single-group
strengths keep the comparison small, and **no permutation p-values are
calculated**. The species used to fit or choose a map cannot then provide an
independent test of its quality (De Cáceres and Legendre, 2009).

```{r}
#| label: compare-habitat-maps

diagnostic.columns = c("elevation_m", "slope_deg", "tpi_m")
minimum.indicator.abundance = 50L

# Keep only maps that you fitted. This list is the sole method-specific edit.
maps <- list(legacy = habitat.raw, standardized = habitat.hclust,
	fanny.hard = habitat.fanny, floristic.tree = habitat.ctree)
diagnostic.environment <- scale(environment[, diagnostic.columns, drop = FALSE])
diagnostic.distance <- dist(diagnostic.environment)
diagnostic.species <- colSums(composition) >= minimum.indicator.abundance
diagnostics <- data.frame(method = names(maps), habitats = NA_integer_,
	smallest.class = NA_integer_, largest.class = NA_integer_,
	environment.silhouette = NA_real_, environment.within.fraction = NA_real_,
	mean.best.indicator = NA_real_)
indicator.strength <- vector("list", length(maps))
names(indicator.strength) <- names(maps)
total.ss <- sum(scale(diagnostic.environment, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)^2)

for(j in seq_along(maps))
{
	if(!is.null(names(maps[[j]])))
		stopifnot(identical(names(maps[[j]]), rownames(composition)))
	groups <- match(as.character(maps[[j]]), unique(as.character(maps[[j]])))
	stopifnot(length(groups) == nrow(composition), !anyNA(groups))
	sizes <- tabulate(groups)
	diagnostics$habitats[j] <- length(sizes)
	diagnostics$smallest.class[j] <- min(sizes)
	diagnostics$largest.class[j] <- max(sizes)
	if(length(sizes) > 1 && length(sizes) < length(groups))
		diagnostics$environment.silhouette[j] <-
			mean(silhouette(groups, diagnostic.distance)[, "sil_width"])
	centres <- rowsum(diagnostic.environment, groups) / sizes
	within.ss <- sum((diagnostic.environment - centres[groups, , drop = FALSE])^2)
	diagnostics$environment.within.fraction[j] <- within.ss / total.ss
	indicator.strength[[j]] <- strassoc(composition[, diagnostic.species, drop = FALSE],
		cluster = groups, func = "IndVal.g")
	diagnostics$mean.best.indicator[j] <-
		mean(apply(indicator.strength[[j]], 1, max))
}
print(diagnostics, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

This common-space silhouette differs from the FANNY selection diagnostic if its
distance or PCA options differ. The within-class fraction is a description in
the declared standardized space, not out-of-sample prediction error. Compare
environmental profiles and class areas as well as these numbers. Changing the
number of classes or retained species changes the opportunities for a strong
indicator. For M > 1, report each assemblage's size and k separately; do not
compare indicator strength across different populations as a controlled method
comparison.

For a bounded sensitivity analysis, change **one** consequential choice: for
example, compare k = 3, 4 and 5 at fixed predictors, or include one soil variable
at fixed k. Keep the same eligible population. Record whether environmental
interpretation and association conclusions change, including the cost of small
classes. A later census assesses temporal robustness when prepared with the
same rules. Predictive tuning requires held-out spatial blocks and all
preprocessing fitted within each training fold; ordinary leave-one-quadrat-out
validation can be optimistic under spatial dependence (Roberts et al., 2017).
Neither this table nor a torus test validates the entire map-selection process.


# Species–habitat association with a fixed map {#sec-association}

Use a map defined from environmental information, fixed before examining the
focal species. Indicator strengths above describe a map; the following spatial
randomization asks whether observed species shares depart from random alignment
with that map. Selecting a floristically fitted map changes this interpretation.

## Set up an independent fixed-map analysis

Read these ordinary objects directly if they were saved earlier; fitted
classifiers and environmental rasters are not required here.

| Object | Required contents |
|---|---|
| `quadrats` | Complete Cartesian rectangular tiling with `quadrat_id`, `xmin`, `xmax`, `ymin`, `ymax`; include empty quadrats. |
| `composition` | Quadrat-by-species individual-count matrix for all eligible species; row names equal `quadrats$quadrat_id` in order. |
| `habitats` | One fixed, nonmissing class per quadrat, aligned with `composition`. |
| `individuals` | One row per eligible individual with `x`, `y`, `species`; the same population that produced `composition`. |
| `plot.extent` | Known bounds `c(xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)` in the same coordinate system. |

The following optional entry chunk starts a new script from the checkpoint
above. Set real paths first; otherwise continue with the objects already in
memory. It needs only base R and the original translator, not the classifiers.
For your own map, supply the same objects directly and declare whether the test
flora helped fit **or select** it.

```{r}
#| label: restart-fixed-map-analysis
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Start a separate script from saved ordinary objects"

path.to.fgeo2 = "/full/path/to/fgeo2"
fixed.map.file = "/full/path/to/fixed-map-inputs.rds"

inputs <- readRDS(fixed.map.file)
quadrats <- inputs$quadrats
composition <- inputs$composition
habitats <- inputs$habitats
individuals <- inputs$individuals
plot.extent <- inputs$plot.extent
map.uses.test.flora <- inputs$map.uses.test.flora
source(file.path(path.to.fgeo2, "03_spatial/R/new/spatial-null-models.R"))
```

Prepare **one census and one eligible population**, resolving multiple stems,
status and dbh limits beforehand. Selecting focal species below does not remove
other species from the community background. For a dbh-specific analysis, first
regenerate both community inputs for that class. Do not infer plot bounds from
occupied tree locations.

The existing `translate_around_torus()` returns one matrix per coordinate
dimension, with points in rows and simulations in columns. We request one
simulation per iteration and keep the habitat map fixed. All marked individuals
receive the same x displacement and the same y displacement. This preserves
species totals and within- and between-species **toroidal** geometry. Ordinary
Euclidean distances across the wrapped rectangle's edges need not be preserved.
There are no reflections, rotations or separate shifts for different species.

The null is random alignment of this intact community with the map under uniform
continuous translations. Its interpretation requires translation exchangeability;
a rectangle alone does not establish stationarity or ecological periodicity.
Inspect directional trends and artificial joins across opposite edges. Missing
habitat cells and irregular plot masks require another explicit null design;
this example rejects them rather than dropping translated points.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

## Check a small rectangle by hand

For $[10,18)\times[20,24)$, shifting $(15,21)$ by $(3,1)$ gives $(10,22)$.
Initially each habitat contains three individuals: A's relative-density ratios
are `(2, 0)`, B's are `(0, 2)` and C's are `(1, 1)`.

```{r}
#| label: torus-rectangular-check

# Use the repository path configured in setup or the independent entry.
source(file.path(path.to.fgeo2, "03_spatial/R/new/spatial-null-models.R"))

toy.xy <- cbind(x = c(11, 12, 15, 16, 13, 17),
                y = c(21, 23, 21, 23, 21, 23))
toy.species <- c("A", "A", "B", "B", "C", "C")
toy.mins = c(10, 20)
toy.maxs = c(18, 24)
toy.step = c(3, 1)
toy.wrapped <- toy.xy
for(d in 1:2)
	toy.wrapped[, d] <- toy.mins[d] +
		(toy.xy[, d] + toy.step[d] - toy.mins[d]) %% (toy.maxs[d] - toy.mins[d])
stopifnot(all(toy.wrapped == cbind(c(14, 15, 10, 11, 16, 12),
                                  c(22, 20, 22, 20, 22, 20))))
toy.counts <- table(toy.species, habitat = ifelse(toy.xy[, 1] < 14, "left", "right"))
toy.ratio <- sweep(sweep(toy.counts, 2, colSums(toy.counts), "/"),
                   1, rowSums(toy.counts) / sum(toy.counts), "/")
stopifnot(all(toy.ratio == rbind(c(2, 0), c(0, 2), c(1, 1))))
toy.shifted.counts <- table(toy.species,
                            habitat = ifelse(toy.wrapped[, 1] < 14, "left", "right"))
stopifnot(all(toy.shifted.counts == rbind(c(0, 2), c(2, 0), c(1, 1))))
toy.counts
toy.ratio

# Reproduce the existing translator's random steps; verify shared displacements.
set.seed(904)
toy.random.step <- c(runif(1, 0, 8), runif(1, 0, 4))
set.seed(904)
toy.translation <- translate_around_torus(toy.xy, mins = toy.mins,
                                         maxs = toy.maxs, nsim = 1)
for(d in 1:2)
	stopifnot(max(abs((toy.translation[[d]][, 1] - toy.xy[, d]) %%
	                 (toy.maxs[d] - toy.mins[d]) - toy.random.step[d])) < 1e-10)
```
:::

## Specify the statistic

Let $n_{sh}$ be species $s$'s individual count in habitat $h$, $n_h$ the count of
**all eligible individuals** there, $n_s$ its plot-wide count and $n$ the community
total. The [legacy `tt_test()` source](https://github.com/forestgeo/fgeo.analyze/blob/d69bfe711263305fcbaf322d402eba2f1edfb084/R/tt_test.R)
calculates `spstcnthab / totstcnthab`, or $n_{sh}/n_h$, recomputing both counts for
each translated map. We divide it by the species' constant plot-wide frequency:

$$R_{sh}=\frac{n_{sh}/n_h}{n_s/n}.$$

This rescaling preserves its ordering across shifts. Two means twice the
plot-wide species share. One is a composition reference, not necessarily the mean
of the simulated ratios. Our continuous point shifts differ from the legacy
exhaustive quadrat-map shifts and reflections: these are not identical nulls.

The alternative `"area_density"` uses $R^{\mathrm{area}}_{sh}=(n_{sh}/A_h)/(n_s/A)$.
Its fixed area denominator makes testing this ratio equivalent to testing the
species count. It tests species intensity per area, without controlling for
community density. Choose the scientific denominator before running the analysis.

```{r}
#| label: torus-options

nsim = 9999L             # Use 999 for a quick check, with coarser p resolution.
torus.seed = 123L
minimum.abundance = 50L  # Focal reporting filter; background stays complete.
focal.species = NULL     # Or an explicit vector of species codes.
association.statistic = "relative_density"  # Alternative: "area_density".
p.adjust.method = "BH"  # Alternatives: "holm" or "none".
alpha = 0.05

# This worked inference requires a map chosen independently of the test flora.
# For a supplied map, declare map.uses.test.flora explicitly before this chunk.
if(!identical(map.uses.test.flora, FALSE))
	stop("Use an independent fixed map for inference; describe a floristically fitted map separately.")
```

## Align the map, counts and points

The boundary lookup handles arbitrary quadrat-table order. Internal edges belong
to the cell on their right/top; observed points at the outer maximum belong to
the final cell, matching the native left/bottom boundary convention.

```{r}
#| label: torus-align-inputs
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Check alignment and construct the rectangular point lookup"

stopifnot(nsim >= 1, nsim == floor(nsim),
          association.statistic %in% c("relative_density", "area_density"))
composition <- as.matrix(composition)
stopifnot(all(is.finite(composition)), all(composition >= 0),
          all(composition == floor(composition)), !is.null(colnames(composition)),
          !anyNA(colnames(composition)), !anyDuplicated(colnames(composition)),
          !anyNA(quadrats$quadrat_id), !anyDuplicated(quadrats$quadrat_id),
          identical(rownames(composition), as.character(quadrats$quadrat_id)),
          length(habitats) == nrow(quadrats), !anyNA(habitats))
if(!is.null(names(habitats)))
	stopifnot(identical(names(habitats), rownames(composition)))

torus.mins <- plot.extent[c(1, 3)]
torus.maxs <- plot.extent[c(2, 4)]
stopifnot(all(is.finite(plot.extent)), all(torus.maxs > torus.mins),
          all(is.finite(as.matrix(quadrats[c("xmin", "xmax", "ymin", "ymax")]))),
          all(quadrats$xmax > quadrats$xmin), all(quadrats$ymax > quadrats$ymin))
x.breaks <- sort(unique(c(quadrats$xmin, quadrats$xmax)))
y.breaks <- sort(unique(c(quadrats$ymin, quadrats$ymax)))
nx <- length(x.breaks) - 1L
ny <- length(y.breaks) - 1L
qx <- match(quadrats$xmin, x.breaks)
qy <- match(quadrats$ymin, y.breaks)
cell <- qx + (qy - 1L) * nx
stopifnot(nrow(quadrats) == nx * ny, !anyDuplicated(cell),
          all(quadrats$xmax == x.breaks[qx + 1L]),
          all(quadrats$ymax == y.breaks[qy + 1L]),
          all(c(x.breaks[1], tail(x.breaks, 1)) == plot.extent[1:2]),
          all(c(y.breaks[1], tail(y.breaks, 1)) == plot.extent[3:4]))
cell.to.quadrat <- integer(nx * ny)
cell.to.quadrat[cell] <- seq_len(nrow(quadrats))

coordinates <- as.matrix(individuals[c("x", "y")])
species.i <- match(as.character(individuals$species), colnames(composition))
stopifnot(nrow(individuals) > 0, all(is.finite(coordinates)), !anyNA(species.i),
          all(individuals$x >= torus.mins[1] & individuals$x <= torus.maxs[1]),
          all(individuals$y >= torus.mins[2] & individuals$y <= torus.maxs[2]))
ix <- pmin(findInterval(individuals$x, x.breaks), nx)
iy <- pmin(findInterval(individuals$y, y.breaks), ny)
quadrat.i <- cell.to.quadrat[ix + (iy - 1L) * nx]
point.counts <- matrix(tabulate(quadrat.i + (species.i - 1L) * nrow(quadrats),
                                nbins = length(composition)), nrow = nrow(quadrats))
if(!all(point.counts == composition))
	stop("individuals and composition describe different populations or quadrat assignments")

species.total <- colSums(composition)
if(is.null(focal.species))
	focal.species <- names(sort(species.total[species.total >= minimum.abundance],
	                            decreasing = TRUE))
stopifnot(length(focal.species) > 0, !anyNA(focal.species),
          !anyDuplicated(focal.species), all(focal.species %in% colnames(composition)),
          all(species.total[focal.species] > 0))
habitat.levels <- sort(unique(as.character(habitats)))
habitat.i <- match(as.character(habitats), habitat.levels)
nh <- length(habitat.levels)
nf <- length(focal.species)
n.total <- nrow(individuals)
focal.total <- as.numeric(species.total[focal.species])
focal.i <- match(as.character(individuals$species), focal.species)
focal.points <- !is.na(focal.i)
habitat.area <- as.numeric(rowsum((quadrats$xmax - quadrats$xmin) *
                                   (quadrats$ymax - quadrats$ymin), habitat.i))
observed.habitat <- habitat.i[quadrat.i]
observed.community <- tabulate(observed.habitat, nbins = nh)
observed.counts <- matrix(tabulate(focal.i[focal.points] +
                                    (observed.habitat[focal.points] - 1L) * nf,
                                  nbins = nf * nh), nrow = nf)
observed.relative <- sweep(sweep(observed.counts, 2, observed.community, "/"),
                           1, focal.total / n.total, "/")
area.expected <- outer(focal.total, habitat.area / sum(habitat.area))
observed.statistic <- observed.relative
if(association.statistic == "area_density")
	observed.statistic <- observed.counts / area.expected
```

## Shift the intact marked community

Store the small focal-species-by-habitat-by-simulation statistic array, not all
translated coordinates. For 250 species, four habitats and 9,999 simulations this
array occupies about 80 MB. Other calculations need additional working memory.
Each iteration recomputes the habitat's **whole-community** denominator.

```{r}
#| label: torus-simulation

null.statistics <- array(NA_real_, dim = c(nf, nh, nsim),
                          dimnames = list(focal.species, habitat.levels, NULL))
set.seed(torus.seed)
for(b in seq_len(nsim))
{
	translated <- translate_around_torus(coordinates, mins = torus.mins,
	                                     maxs = torus.maxs, nsim = 1)
	ix <- pmin(findInterval(translated[[1]][, 1], x.breaks), nx)
	iy <- pmin(findInterval(translated[[2]][, 1], y.breaks), ny)
	translated.habitat <- habitat.i[cell.to.quadrat[ix + (iy - 1L) * nx]]
	sim.community <- tabulate(translated.habitat, nbins = nh)
	sim.counts <- matrix(tabulate(focal.i[focal.points] +
	                               (translated.habitat[focal.points] - 1L) * nf,
	                             nbins = nf * nh), nrow = nf)
	stopifnot(sum(sim.community) == n.total, all(rowSums(sim.counts) == focal.total))
	null.statistics[, , b] <- sweep(sweep(sim.counts, 2, sim.community, "/"),
	                                1, focal.total / n.total, "/")
	if(association.statistic == "area_density")
		null.statistics[, , b] <- sim.counts / area.expected
}
null.statistics[!is.finite(null.statistics)] <- NA_real_
```

## Summarize evidence, including unresolved cases

With $B$ shifts, enrichment is $(1+\#\{R^{(b)}\geq R^{\mathrm{obs}}\})/(B+1)$;
depletion uses $\leq$. Ties enter both tails; p-values cannot be zero. Double the
smaller tail, capped at one, before adjusting one two-sided test per table row.

An empty community in a habitat makes its relative-density statistic undefined.
Count these shifts without redrawing, and withhold affected p-values even if only
one shift was undefined. Finite-draw summaries are then partial. Consider the
scientifically different area/count statistic or a predeclared broader population
or less fragmented map, and restart; do not condition silently on nonempty habitats.

```{r}
#| label: torus-results

association <- expand.grid(species = focal.species, habitat = habitat.levels,
                            KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
association$n.sh <- as.vector(observed.counts)
association$n.h <- rep(observed.community, each = nf)
association$n.s <- rep(focal.total, times = nh)
association$n.total <- n.total
association$habitat.area <- rep(habitat.area, each = nf)
association$effect.ratio <- as.vector(observed.statistic)
association$statistic <- association.statistic
association$null.n <- as.vector(apply(is.finite(null.statistics), c(1, 2), sum))
association$undefined.shifts <- nsim - association$null.n
association$null.mean <- as.vector(apply(null.statistics, c(1, 2), mean, na.rm = TRUE))
association$null.sd <- as.vector(apply(null.statistics, c(1, 2), sd, na.rm = TRUE))
null.quantiles <- apply(null.statistics, c(1, 2), quantile,
                        probs = c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975), na.rm = TRUE)
association$null.q025 <- as.vector(null.quantiles[1, , ])
association$null.median <- as.vector(null.quantiles[2, , ])
association$null.q975 <- as.vector(null.quantiles[3, , ])
association$null.mean[association$null.n == 0] <- NA_real_

null.difference <- sweep(null.statistics, c(1, 2), observed.statistic, "-")
association$p.enrichment <- (1 + as.vector(apply(null.difference >= 0,
                                                c(1, 2), sum, na.rm = TRUE))) / (nsim + 1)
association$p.depletion <- (1 + as.vector(apply(null.difference <= 0,
                                               c(1, 2), sum, na.rm = TRUE))) / (nsim + 1)
complete.null <- is.finite(association$effect.ratio) & association$null.n == nsim
association$p.enrichment[!complete.null] <- association$p.depletion[!complete.null] <- NA_real_
association$p.two.sided <- pmin(1, 2 * pmin(association$p.enrichment, association$p.depletion))
association$p.adjusted <- p.adjust(association$p.two.sided, method = p.adjust.method,
                                    n = nrow(association))
association$status <- "inconclusive"
association$status[!complete.null] <- "undefined statistic"
association$status[which(association$p.adjusted <= alpha &
                           association$p.enrichment < association$p.depletion)] <- "enriched versus shifts"
association$status[which(association$p.adjusted <= alpha &
                           association$p.depletion < association$p.enrichment)] <- "depleted versus shifts"
data.frame(simulations = nsim, family.tests = nrow(association),
           minimum.two.sided.p = min(1, 2 / (nsim + 1)),
           first.rank.threshold = alpha / nrow(association))
table(association$status)
species.preferences <- matrix(association$status, nrow = nf,
	dimnames = list(species = focal.species, habitat = habitat.levels))
# Keep the complete association table; print a short, readable view.
report.columns <- c("species", "habitat", "n.sh", "effect.ratio",
	"p.two.sided", "p.adjusted", "status")
head(association[order(association$p.adjusted, na.last = TRUE), report.columns], 12)
```

In this run, `r sum(association$status == "enriched versus shifts")` pairs are
enriched, `r sum(association$status == "depleted versus shifts")` depleted and
`r sum(association$status == "inconclusive")` inconclusive after BH adjustment.
For the supplied defaults, code `ouralu` is depleted in class 2 (ratio 0.36)
and enriched in class 4 (ratio 1.51), both with adjusted p about 0.026. A species
can therefore have different associations with several parts of the same map;
the result is not a single exclusive habitat label per species.

`association` is the full table; null quantiles are distribution summaries, not
confidence intervals. Enrichment/depletion refers to the shift distribution;
above/below one refers to the chosen density reference. Inconclusive does not mean
neutrality or ecological equivalence. With 999 shifts the minimum two-sided p is
0.002; 500 tests give a first BH/Holm threshold of 0.0001 at $\alpha=0.05$, too
small for an isolated discovery. BH can retain a sufficiently large set of small
p-values. More shifts improve resolution, not the validity of the ecological null.
For these BCI defaults there are 1,164 species–habitat tests. A 999-shift trial
left all of them inconclusive after BH adjustment; the longer run improves
Monte Carlo resolution while retaining exactly the same map and species family.

BH's usual false-discovery-rate guarantees require independence or suitable
positive dependence, not automatically provided here. Holm controls family-wise
error under arbitrary dependence when the underlying p-values are valid. `"none"`
leaves p-values unadjusted. None repairs selection of the map, species, $M$ or $k$
after inspecting associations. The main table tests single habitats: searching
for the best habitat union requires repeating that search inside every null draw,
or testing all prespecified unions within the declared family.

## Inspect two example null distributions

```{r}
#| label: torus-null-diagnostics
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.5

previous.par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
for(i in seq_len(min(2, nrow(association))))
{
	values <- null.statistics[association$species[i], association$habitat[i], ]
	values <- values[is.finite(values)]
	if(length(values) == 0) next
	hist(values, breaks = 20, col = "grey85", border = "white",
	     xlim = range(c(values, association$effect.ratio[i]), finite = TRUE),
	     xlab = association.statistic,
	     main = paste(association$species[i], "habitat", association$habitat[i]))
	if(is.finite(association$effect.ratio[i]))
		abline(v = association$effect.ratio[i], col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
}
par(previous.par)
```

The red line marks the observation. These fixed example panels do not search for
the strongest association. The test assesses alignment under the specified null;
it does not establish an optimal map, discrete rather than continuous habitats,
or a causal effect of habitat on species distribution.

# Reuse the results

Save the selected labels, preprocessing choices and native fitted object rather
than only a coloured figure. The checkpoint retains point coordinates because
another association analysis may need them. For long-term storage, GeoTIFF
layers and their class keys complement the ordinary R objects; do not serialize
a live `SpatRaster` with a bare `saveRDS()` and expect its external pointer to
survive another session. Use `writeRaster()` as shown above, or `terra::wrap()`
when an R-only representation is needed.

```{r}
#| label: save-habitat-results

results.file = file.path(output.dir, "habitat-analysis.rds")

# This final checkpoint requires the completed analysis; map-only users use
# fixed-map-inputs.rds above instead.
saveRDS(list(quadrats = quadrats, environment = environment,
	composition = composition, individuals = individuals, plot.extent = plot.extent,
	habitats = habitats, models = models, association = association,
	null.statistics = null.statistics, species.preferences = species.preferences,
	settings = list(census = census.file, minimum.dbh.cm = minimum.dbh.cm,
		quadrat.size = quadrat.size, selected.map = selected.map,
		classification.columns = selected.features,
		torus.seed = torus.seed, nsim = nsim, statistic = association.statistic,
		p.adjust.method = p.adjust.method)), results.file)
sessionInfo()
```

The saved setting names describe this demonstration. Update them when changing
the selected map or preprocessing. An inconclusive species result does not
establish ecological equivalence. A floristically informed classification
describes the population used to fit it; independent species testing requires a
design that separates fitting and testing, or a null that repeats the relevant
fitting/selection procedure. A later census of surviving trees alone does not
create that independence.

# Further options and scope

The core deliberately keeps M = 1, hard labels for inference, and one complete
rectangular plot. The two diameter groups illustrate user-controlled M without
inventing an assemblage-discovery algorithm. Species groups can also be supplied
from traits or an independently justified composition/co-occurrence analysis;
crossing these with a few diameter classes gives species × size assemblages.
Sparse groups may support no useful split. Optimizing their definitions is a
separate research problem with another layer of selection to validate.

Other well-supported directions include mixed environmental distances with
`cluster::daisy()`, ordination and continuous composition models in `vegan`,
and spatially constrained classification in `adespatial`. Euclidean Ward
clustering requires an appropriate Euclidean representation; constrained trees
and spatial smoothing express different objectives. Fuzzy class affiliation is
not a substitute for bootstrapping a classifier's stability. A partition fitted
in one plot is not automatically a transferable habitat definition, and
hierarchical clustering itself supplies no environmental prediction rule for
new sites. The conditional tree does provide such a rule, subject to covariate
coverage and external validation.

The literature review also considered spatial extent separately from quadrat
grain (Garzon-Lopez et al., 2014), sampling artefacts in regional mixture models
(Foster et al., 2017), and species-combination indicators (De Cáceres et al.,
2012). Those extensions are not added to the executable core. Detailed map
styling and reusable plotting helpers belong in `07_mapping_plotting`.
